chapter: Learning from players; Jonah Jones lessons
title: Cootie Williams and the foot-tapping cure
summary: Cootie advises Maxwell to practice with both feet marching, using Arban exercise 10.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: But over the years I've been lucky to work with people like him I could learn things from. Like Cootie I learned an awful lot from. From the day I first met him in San Francisco when I was still in high school, 1932 or something --

Yeah. I went backstage and introduced myself. That was awful nervy, you know. Cootie was sitting there practicing and Freddie Jenkins was sitting there practicing. I remember I still could see the book, they had a little band book for band players, exercises for band musicians. And I was so surprised to see jazz musicians practicing. And

naturally, Freddie is going through all kinds of technical exercises, double tongue and (humming). And Cootie is playing very solid, straight-ahead, you know how he plays, he's got the greatest time feel in the world, I think. And even when I was in Benny Goodman's band, I had a very bad period there, I never used to beat my foot. I used to dance when I played, you know, my feet would hop around. And Clark does that, he drives me crazy, his feet keep dancing around.

And Benny saw that one time and he looked at it and he laughed, he would point out my feet. Everytime he would look up he'd laugh. And he got me in such a state that I couldn't play, I couldn't keep time. And I was seriously considering going to a psychiatrist, I was getting desperate. And Cootie finally decided to take over, he was always giving me advice, being my elder. We roomed together a lot on the road, and Cootie showed me how he was -- Cootie would keep both feet like he was marching, you know. Left foot would be one and three; right foot two and four. And he said, just keep the feet going like that and nobody can shake you. And he was right. It took a little -- I said, I can't get used to it, he said, get out Arban. So we got out Arban and he said, there's an exercise in Arban, it's number 10 --
Yeah, that's the trumpet player's bible, a very legitimate little one, went (humming). And I was about

to laugh and then I thought, what are you laughing about? Why shouldn't you practice the way you play, it makes sense. So I practiced my Arban, beating both feet. And I've been doing that for 40 years, that's one of the greatest things. I don't care who the drummer is, they couldn't shake me because I get both feet going. And you could get one of the most wandering drummers in the world --
